title: What Causes Pastor Burnout, and How Do You Recover?
subtitle: There is a difference between laying your life down and letting it be taken, and the tired pastor has usually forgotten which one he agreed to.
group: The Inner Life of the Leader

sections.title: Burnout Wears the Costume of Faithfulness
sections.body:
No one burns out doing what they hate. You burn out doing what you love, past the place where love was supposed to stop. That is what makes it so hard to see coming. It does not arrive looking like sin. It arrives looking like devotion.

I ran myself into the ground once and called it sacrifice. Sixty, seventy hours a week. Skipped days off, missed dinners, a phone that never went dark. And the whole time I felt righteous about it, because the church was being served and I was the one serving it, and who corrects a man for working too hard for God. No one. They thank him. They hold him up as an example. They drive him toward the cliff with applause.

Not all of that was love for the church. Some of it was fear. Fear that if I stopped, the thing would fall, which is another way of saying I believed the thing was held up by me. That is not faith. That is the opposite of faith wearing faith's clothes.

sections.title: Laid Down, or Taken
sections.body:
Jesus said no one takes my life from me, I lay it down of my own accord. Read that slowly. He was the most poured-out man who ever lived, and he insisted that the pouring was a choice he made, not a theft he suffered.

The burned-out pastor has lost that distinction. He is not laying his life down. He is letting it be taken, a little at every meeting, by every demand, until there is nothing left to give and he resents the people he is supposed to love. A life laid down is given from fullness, on purpose, with the giver in possession of himself. A life taken is bled out by drift, by inability to say no, by the slow surrender of every boundary until the man is a hollow that says yes to everyone.

Jesus withdrew. The crowds were still sick and he went to the mountain to pray. He let people stay in need while he attended to his own soul, and he did it without apology and without guilt. The pastor who cannot do that has confused himself with the Messiah, and it is the most exhausting heresy there is.

sections.title: Rest Is Not a Reward, It Is a Command
sections.body:
We treat rest as something you earn after the work is done. But the work is never done. The hospital list never empties. The needs never stop. If rest waits for the work to be finished, rest never comes, and the pastor dies at his desk believing he was being faithful.

The Sabbath was not a reward for the productive. It was a command, and it came with a threat, because God knew we would not take it on our own. He built the rhythm into creation and then into law because he understood that a man who will not stop is a man who has made himself God, and that man must be stopped before he breaks himself and everyone leaning on him.

Sustainability is not the opposite of obedience. It is a form of it. The pastor who guards a day off, who keeps a real Sabbath, who sleeps and eats and walks and plays with his children, is obeying. The pastor who burns through all of it is not more obedient. He is more disobedient, in a way the church will praise him for, which is the cruelest trap of all.

sections.title: What to Actually Do Before You Break
sections.body:
Here is the concrete part, because exhortation alone has never rescued a tired man. These are not tips. They are protections, and you build them before you need them.

Take a day off and defend it like a marriage. One full day, same day each week, phone off, no exceptions you would not make for a heart attack. If an emergency genuinely arises, fine, but most of what feels like an emergency is only someone else's poor planning becoming your crisis. Let it wait. The church survived before you and will survive your day off.

Name the three things only you can do, and give the rest away. You are not the only one who can set up chairs, answer that email, run that committee. You may be the only one who can preach Sunday and shepherd the dying. Protect those. Release the rest, even imperfectly, even to people who will do it worse than you. Done worse by someone else beats done well by a man in the grave.

Watch the early warnings, because burnout announces itself. Cynicism about the people you serve. A short fuse at home. Loss of joy in prayer. Dreading Sunday. When those arrive, they are not character flaws to push through. They are the dashboard light, and you stop the car when it comes on, not after the engine seizes.

sections.title: The Man Who Could Not Stop
sections.body:
I knew a pastor who could not stop. Good man, real gift, loved his people. He worked the way I once worked, and the church grew, and everyone admired his stamina. He died at fifty-eight of a heart his doctor had warned him about for years. At the funeral they called him a faithful servant who gave everything for the kingdom.

I sat in that service and could not say amen. He did not give everything for the kingdom. He gave everything because he could not trust the kingdom to stand without him. He gave his wife a husband she barely saw and his sons a father made of fatigue, and he called it sacrifice, and we let him, because his collapse looked like our idea of a hero.

I am not certain I would have done any better. That is why I am writing this with my own warning lights in view. The tired shepherd does not need another exhortation to work harder. He needs permission, in the name of the God who rested, to stop before he is taken.

Lay it down. Do not let it be taken. There is a difference, and your family will feel which one you chose long after you are gone.
